collections.title: Protecting our pond banks
collections.dek: Three ponds, one storm, and the slow work of putting the edges back.

stories.title: A planting day on the Big Pond
stories.dek: Forty pots, a wheelbarrow of mulch, and the Wednesday crew.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. One Wednesday afternoon, the Bright Futures crew put a hundred plants into the bank of the Big Pond.

stories.title: Helen Lewis, with a long lens
stories.dek: Most of the birds on this site were photographed by one person, on foot, before breakfast.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. Helen walks the park early with a long lens. The birds on this site are mostly hers.

stories.title: The palm collection nobody knew we had
stories.dek: Decades of quiet buying at estate sales left us with one of the better palm collections on the coast.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. Nobody set out to build a palm collection. It happened one estate sale at a time.

stories.title: The plants we chose, and why
stories.dek: Salt wind above, wet feet below, and nothing that needs a hose.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. A pond bank is two gardens in one: the strip that floods and the strip that only gets the wind.

stories.title: Winter visitors
stories.dek: The American White Pelicans come in December and leave before the heat. The Big Pond is on their route.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. Some winters a flock of white pelicans settles on the Big Pond and feeds in a line, like a net being drawn.

stories.title: Why the banks needed work
stories.dek: Salt water does not look like damage until the following spring.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. The storm surge came and went in a night. The pond edges took a year to show what it had done.

stories.title: After the storms
stories.dek: Three hurricanes in two seasons, and what each one left behind.
stories.teaser: SAMPLE. Wind takes the tops off trees. Salt takes the roots. It took us a season to learn which storm had done what.
